content: Smoking in adulthood often begins during adolescence. If individuals do not start smoking during this critical period, it is unlikely they will ever begin. However, once smoking becomes a habit, quitting becomes increasingly difficult, with the likelihood of cessation decreasing the earlier smoking is initiated. One innovative strategy to reduce youth smoking is the use of incentive-based programs. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of incentives in preventing smoking initiation among children and adolescents aged 5 to 18 years. Additionally, the review aimed to explore the dose-response relationship of incentives, the costs associated with such programs, the potential effectiveness of combining incentives with other interventions, and any unintended consequences that might arise from their use. For the original review, published in 2012, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Tobacco Addiction Group Specialized Register, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, CSA databases, and PsycINFO. The most recent search was performed in December 2016. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and controlled trials (CTs) that allocated children and adolescents to either intervention or control groups, where the intervention involved incentives aimed at preventing smoking initiation. Studies required a minimum follow-up period of six months, and the primary outcome was the smoking status of participants who reported being non-smokers at baseline. Two authors independently extracted and assessed the data, evaluating the risk of bias in each study. The most stringent definition of smoking abstinence was used for analysis, though biochemical validation of self-reported tobacco use was not required for inclusion. Where possible, data from eligible studies were pooled using the Mantel-Haenszel fixed-effect method, with studies grouped by design. The review identified three RCTs and five CTs, involving participants aged 11 to 14 years who were non-smokers at baseline. Of these, six studies provided analyzable data, contributing to meta-analyses with a total of 7,275 participants (4,003 in intervention groups and 3,272 in control groups; 2,484 participants after adjusting for clustering). Most of the studies evaluated the Smokefree Class Competition (SFC), a program widely implemented in Europe. In the SFC, classes of students aged 11 to 14 committed to remaining smoke-free for six months, with regular reporting of their smoking status. If 90% or more of the class remained non-smokers at the end of the period, they were entered into a competition to win prizes. One study, not involving the SFC, assigned schools in two communities to an intervention group, with a third community serving as a control. In this study, students in the intervention group received rewards if their smoking rates were lower at the end of the school year. The results of most studies were statistically non-significant. Only one SFC study reported a significant effect on smoking prevention at the longest follow-up, but this study was at high risk of multiple biases. When the adjusted risk ratio (RR) was calculated, the significant effect was no longer observed. The pooled RR from the more robust RCTs (three studies, 3,056 participants; 1,107 adjusted for clustering) indicated no statistically significant effect of incentives, such as the SFC, on preventing smoking initiation among children and adolescents in the long term (RR 1.00, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.84 to 1.19). Similarly, pooled results from non-randomized trials did not show a significant effect of the SFC, and data on the primary outcome could not be extracted from the one study that did not evaluate the SFC. There was limited evidence to suggest that unintended consequences, such as false reporting of smoking status or bullying of smoking students, were consistently associated with these interventions. However, this aspect has not been extensively studied. Additionally, there was insufficient information to assess the dose-response relationship or the costs of incentive programs aimed at preventing smoking initiation. The included RCTs were judged to be at unclear risk of bias, while the non-RCTs were at high risk of bias. Using the GRADE system, the overall quality of evidence for the primary outcome was rated as low for RCTs and very low for non-RCTs, due to imprecision (wide confidence intervals in all studies) and identified risks of bias. The non-RCT evidence was further downgraded due to inherent design limitations likely to introduce additional bias. In conclusion, the limited evidence available suggests that incentive programs, such as the SFC, do not effectively prevent smoking initiation among youth. However, the number of published studies is small, and their quality is variable. Furthermore, all trials included in the meta-analyses evaluated the SFC, which involved small to moderately-sized prizes distributed to entire classes, often through a lottery system. It is possible that other types of incentive programs could be more effective in preventing smoking initiation among young people. Future research should explore a broader range of incentive strategies, including those targeting individual participants, and assess their impact on both smoking initiation and progression to regular smoking. It would also be beneficial to evaluate these programs in diverse populations, considering varying socioeconomic and ethnic backgrounds, and to provide detailed descriptions of intervention components.
